place-value.title: Place value: where a digit sits is what it is worth
place-value.recall: Cover the picture. What is the 7 worth in 2,740? And what does borrowing swap?

frames.caption: 345 is 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 5 ones — say what each digit is WORTH, not just what it is.
Each column is worth ten times the one on its right.
Ten of one column make one of the next — that is all borrowing and carrying are.

integers.title: Negative numbers on the number line
integers.recall: Cover it. Which way do you move for + (−3)? What is 2 − (−5)?

frames.caption: Start at −2. Adding 5 moves you five steps to the right: you land on 3.
Adding a negative number is the same as subtracting: you move left.
Taking away a negative turns you round: −(−4) is +4.

equal-groups.title: Multiplication is equal groups; division undoes it
equal-groups.recall: Cover it. Draw 2 × 6 as an array in your head. What is 20 ÷ 6, with its remainder?

frames.caption: 3 × 4 means three equal groups of four.
Lay the groups out as an array and turn it: the order of a multiplication does not change the answer.
Division asks how many equal groups fit; what cannot make a whole group is the remainder.

fractions.title: Equivalent fractions: cut finer, the amount stays
fractions.recall: Cover it. Give two fractions equal to 3/4. Why is 2/6 the same as 1/3?

frames.caption: A fraction is a number of equal parts: 1/2 is one of two.
Cut each half in two: twice as many parts, twice as many shaded — the same amount.
Multiply (or divide) the top and the bottom by the same number and the fraction is unchanged.

fdp.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages are one number
fdp.recall: Cover it. Write 3/4 as a decimal and a percent. What is 0.1 as a fraction?

frames.caption: Percent means 'out of a hundred'. 25 of these 100 squares are shaded.
The same shaded amount is 1/4, 0.25 and 25%.
Divide to get the decimal; multiply by 100 to get the percent.

bodmas.title: Order of operations
bodmas.recall: Cover it. Say BODMAS from memory. What is 10 − 6 ÷ 2?

frames.caption: Everyone must get the same answer, so there is an agreed order.
Brackets, Orders (powers), then Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction.
Multiply before you add — unless brackets say otherwise.

balance.title: An equation is a balance
balance.recall: Cover it. Solve 2x + 1 = 9 by doing the same to both sides. What did you do first, and why?

frames.caption: x + 3 = 7: the two sides balance.
Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and it stays balanced.
Undo the + 3, and x is on its own: x = 4. Put it back in to check.

like-terms.title: Like terms: only the same kind can be added
like-terms.recall: Cover it. Simplify 5x + 2y − x + y. Why can't 3x and 3x² be added?

frames.caption: Terms are 'like' when the letters match exactly.
Gather each kind together.
Add the numbers in front (coefficients) of each kind. Unlike terms stay apart.

expand.title: Expanding brackets is finding an area

frames.caption: 3(x + 2) is the area of a rectangle 3 tall and x + 2 wide.
Find each part: 3 × x and 3 × 2. Add them: 3x + 6.
Factorising is the same picture backwards: find what both parts share.

indices.title: Laws of indices: count the factors
indices.recall: Cover it. Simplify x⁴ × x³ and y⁶ ÷ y². What is 5⁰, and why?

frames.caption: Write the factors out and count them: 2 + 3 = 5.
Dividing cancels factors: 5 − 2 = 3.
Follow the pattern down: each power is half the last, so anything to the power 0 is 1.

angles.title: Angles on a line, and in a triangle
angles.recall: Cover it. Two angles of a triangle are 70° and 45°. What is the third, and why?

frames.caption: A straight line is a half turn: the angles on it add to 180°.
Take any triangle with angles a, b and c.
Tear off the three corners and put them side by side: they make a straight line, 180°.

pythagoras.title: Pythagoras: the squares on the sides
pythagoras.recall: Cover it. A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse? Which side is c?

frames.caption: A right-angled triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5.
Build a square on each side: 9 small squares and 16 small squares exactly fill the 25.
Only for right-angled triangles. c is always the longest side.

circle.title: Circles: once round is π diameters
circle.recall: Cover it. A wheel has radius 7 cm. How far does it go in one turn (use π ≈ 22/7)?

frames.caption: The radius goes from the centre to the edge; the diameter goes right across.
Roll the circle out flat: its edge is just over three diameters long. That number is π.
Circumference is π × diameter. Area is π × radius squared.

gradient.title: Gradient: rise over run
gradient.recall: Cover it. What is the gradient of y = −3x + 4, and where does it cross the y-axis?

frames.caption: Pick two points on the line. How far across (run)? How far up (rise)?
Gradient is how much it goes up for each one across.
In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is where the line crosses the y-axis.

sohcahtoa.title: Trigonometry: name the sides from the angle
sohcahtoa.hook: SOH CAH TOA — Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent
sohcahtoa.recall: Cover it. Say SOH CAH TOA and what each part means. Which ratio links Opposite and Adjacent?

frames.caption: Stand at the angle θ: the side across from you is Opposite, the one beside you is Adjacent, the longest is the Hypotenuse.
Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent.
Label the sides, choose the ratio from the two you have, then calculate.

mean.title: The mean is levelling out
mean.recall: Cover it. Find the mean of 3, 7, 8 and 10. How is it different from the median?

frames.caption: Five stacks of different heights.
Move cubes from the tall stacks to the short ones until they are all the same height.
That level height is the mean: share the total out equally.

probability.title: Probability: count the equally likely outcomes
probability.recall: Cover it. A bag has 3 red and 5 blue. What is P(red)? P(not red)?

frames.caption: List every outcome. Two dice give 36 equally likely totals in this grid.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ all equally likely outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); the chance something does NOT happen is 1 minus the chance it does.

ratio.title: Sharing in a ratio
ratio.recall: Cover it. Share ₦36 in the ratio 1 : 3. What is one part worth?

frames.caption: A ratio 2 : 3 means 5 equal parts: 2 for one, 3 for the other.
Add the parts, then find what one part is worth.
Multiply each person's parts by one part's value — then check they add up.

interest.title: Simple and compound interest
interest.recall: Cover it. ₦1,000 at 10% for 2 years: what is the simple interest? The compound amount?

frames.caption: Simple interest adds the same amount every year: 10% of what you first put in.
Compound interest pays interest on the interest, so it grows faster each year.
Simple interest is a straight line; compound interest curves upward.

logs.title: A logarithm asks: what power?
logs.recall: Cover it. What is log₂ 32? Write log₁₀ 1000 = 3 as a power.

frames.caption: Raising 2 to a power: 2³ = 8.
A logarithm asks the question backwards: what power of 2 gives 8? Answer: 3.
Every log is a power fact turned round: if bⁿ = x then log_b x = n.

word-classes.title: What job does each word do?
word-classes.recall: Cover it. In 'The old dog barked loudly', name the class of each word.

frames.caption: Look at what each word DOES in the sentence.
A noun names. A verb is the action (or a state, like 'is').
An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb. Decide by the job, not the word.

plurals.title: Making plurals
plurals.recall: Cover it. Give the plurals of fox, lady, key, woman and information.

frames.caption: Most nouns just add -s.
Add -es after s, x, ch, sh (you hear an extra syllable). A consonant + y becomes -ies.
Irregular plurals do not follow the rules — learn them as pairs.

agreement.title: Subject–verb agreement
agreement.recall: Cover it. Choose: 'The list of names (is/are) long.' 'Everybody (know/knows) the answer.'

frames.caption: One subject takes the -s verb; more than one does not.
Cross out the phrase in the middle: the verb agrees with the real subject, 'the box'.
'Each', 'everyone' and 'nobody' are singular. With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

apostrophe.title: The apostrophe: missing letters or belonging
apostrophe.recall: Cover it. Correct: 'The dog wagged it's tail.' 'The two boys bags.'

frames.caption: In a contraction, the apostrophe marks the missing letters.
Write the owner first, then add the apostrophe: one girl's, two girls', the children's.
Test it: if 'it is' fits, write it's. Otherwise it's its — like his and hers, no apostrophe.

homophones.title: There, their, they're — and other sound-alikes
homophones.recall: Cover it. Fill: '___ going to bring ___ books over ___.'

frames.caption: They sound the same; the meaning decides the spelling.
Find the clue inside each word: tHERE, the owner 'I' in thEIR, and the apostrophe in they're.
For any contraction, say the long form; if it fits, use the apostrophe.

tenses.title: Tenses on a timeline
tenses.recall: Cover it. Which tense is 'She has finished'? Draw 'They were playing' on a timeline.

frames.caption: Simple past, present and future: one dot each, at a point in time.
The continuous (be + -ing) is a stretch of time, still going on.
The perfect (have + past participle) is a past action joined to now: 'I have eaten' — so I am not hungry.

passive.title: Active and passive voice
passive.recall: Cover it. Make passive: 'The teacher marked the books.' Make active: 'The match was won by our team.'

frames.caption: Active: the doer (the dog) does the action.
Passive: the receiver comes first, the verb becomes 'was chased', and the doer moves to 'by …' — or disappears.
Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant; otherwise the active is clearer.

reported.title: Reported speech: one step back in time
reported.recall: Cover it. Report: Tobi said, “I will come tomorrow.”

frames.caption: Direct speech gives the exact words.
Reporting moves each tense one step back into the past — and 'today' becomes 'that day'.
Change the person, step the tense back, and drop the quotation marks.

conditionals.title: Conditionals: how likely is the 'if'?
conditionals.recall: Cover it. Finish: 'If I were the principal, I ___.' Which conditional is it?

frames.caption: Zero for facts that are always true; first for a real, likely future.
Second for the imagined; third for a past that cannot be changed.
The further from reality, the further back the tense steps.

articles.title: A or an? Listen, don't look
articles.recall: Cover it. Choose a or an: ___ umbrella, ___ uniform, ___ hour, ___ MP3.

frames.caption: Choose by the first SOUND, not the first letter.
'Hour' starts with a vowel sound; 'university' starts with a 'y' sound.
'A/an' introduces something; 'the' points to one we already know.

stress.title: Word stress can change the word
stress.recall: Cover it. Mark the stress: 'Please conDUCT / CONduct the tests.' Which is the verb?

frames.caption: In every word of two or more syllables, one is stressed: louder, longer, higher.
Many two-syllable pairs stress the first syllable as a noun and the second as a verb.
Stressing a different word in a sentence changes what you mean.

roots.title: Word parts: roots, prefixes and suffixes
roots.hook: Keyword method: link each root to a word you already know — 'tele' as in television
roots.recall: Cover it. What do 'geo', 'graph' and 'auto' mean? Use them to explain 'autograph'.

frames.caption: Many English words are built from Greek and Latin parts. Biology = the study of life.
Learn one root and you can work out a family of words.
A prefix at the front, or a suffix at the end, changes the meaning in a predictable way.

figurative.title: Simile, metaphor, personification
figurative.recall: Cover it. Name each: 'as brave as a lion', 'the classroom was a zoo', 'the car coughed'.

frames.caption: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.
A metaphor says one thing IS another — no 'like' or 'as'.
Personification gives a thing human actions. In an exam, say what effect the comparison has.

peel.title: A strong paragraph: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link
peel.recall: Cover it. Say PEEL from memory, then write a P sentence for 'Phones should be allowed in school'.

frames.caption: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link — one paragraph, one idea.
Each sentence does one job.
Linking words show how one idea leads to the next.

who-whom.title: Who or whom? Swap in he or him
who-whom.hook: whoM = hiM — both end in m
who-whom.recall: Cover it. Choose: 'The man (who/whom) I met was kind.' 'The boy (whose/who's) phone rang left.'

frames.caption: Who does the action (like he); whom receives it (like him). Whom and him both end in m.
Answer the question in your head with he or him, then choose who or whom to match.
Whose shows belonging; which is for things; who's means 'who is'.

punctuation.title: Full stops, commas, semicolons and colons
punctuation.recall: Cover it. Punctuate: 'I was tired I had walked all day' — in two different correct ways.

frames.caption: A full stop ends a sentence; commas separate the items in a list.
A semicolon joins two complete sentences that are closely linked.
A colon says 'here it is': a list, an example or an explanation follows.
